articles.text: The City of Piedmont was selected as a winner of one of the Institute for Local Government’s 2021 Beacon Spotlight Awards. Municipalities receive the award and recognition for sustainability efforts and community greenhouse gas reductions. The Institute for local Government’s (ILG) Beacon Program provides recognition and support for local agencies throughout California that are actively working to build more vibrant and sustainable communities. This is the first year the city has participated in the program. As a participant, the City of Piedmont receives technical assistance in collecting, reporting and tracking sustainability best practices, energy savings and greenhouse gas reductions; access to peer-topeer networking and educational events; and invitations to showcase sustainability leadership and agency achievements to a stateOf the four cities recognized for their collective greenhouse gas emissions reductions, Piedmont led the way with a 30% reduction, followed by Thousand Oaks at 28%, San Rafael at 27%, and Fremont at 26%. Piedmont also received a Gold level award for Agency Greenhouse Gas Reductions of 12%. The city made a commitment to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions five years ago. In 2016, Councilmembers joined the Compact of Mayors, a global coalition of city officials with the common goal of reducing their local greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The initial three-year commitment has led to the adoption of the Climate Action Plan (CAP), which sets a goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 80% below those levels by 2050. Programs that have contributed to progress toward CAP include reach codes, which require that new residential buildings and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) be outfitted with all-electric appliances, and a Home Energy Assessment Policy, now required when listing a property for sale, which helps buyers decide how to best improve a home’s energy use. The Induction Cooktop Lending program will loan residents an electric cooktop for free. It provides education to residents about the benefits of electrifying a kitchen.

articles.text: A research report on homelessness was presented at the recent Fall Reception of East Bay Republican Women. The featured speaker was Mary Theroux, SVP of the Independent Institute, Oakland’s non-profit, non-partisan public policy research and educational organization. She presented her extensive research on the causes and solutions to the homelessness problem. She suggested that childhood trauma is at the root of these dysfunctions, and they will not be solved by housing alone. She questioned the wisdom of the current policy, which focuses exclusively on giving brand-new units to the homeless. She described multi-tiered solutions that have worked in other states, offering levels of treatment and accommodation, while eliminating the option of sleeping on the street.

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department has a brand new addition to its lobby: a three-shelf free book exchange – “Little Free Library” – specifically for young readers age 3 through 11. In the same vein as other traditional free libraries, interested residents may take a book to read or leave one for someone else to find. The “Little Free Library” book exchange relies on volunteer “stewards” to construct, install, and maintain book exchange boxes - they are traditionally placed in front of houses and are supplied through donations from neighborhoods. Officers April Fitzgerald and Nicole Casalnuovo came up with the idea to create a PPD lobby library; and Fitzgerald, a former English teacher, chose to provide the reading exchange specifically for young readers. Officer Tyler Petit and Mo Alrahimi, the Public Works Department’s talented Can-Do man, designed and built the attractive bookcase. “We love it when kids stop by and thought it would be a great way to encourage reading and bring kids to the department so we can connect,” Fitzgerald said. “Even though I’m not in the classroom anymore, that love for teaching and reading doesn’t leave you.” The Police Department’s central location provides for a nice respite to stop and read a book on the way to or back from the park, she added. Passersby can come at any time to drop off a donation - series books, picture books, cardboard books and pop-up books for toddlers are especially welcome. “We’re excited to see what people may bring. My kids have tons and tons of books. So many people have books that they’d like to share, and it’s really a blessing to re-use them,” Fitzgerald said. Kids are encouraged to pick up a reading log when they visit. Fill your child’s reading log with their favorite books and they may even win a prize on their next visit to the department. “It definitely provides a great incentive,” Fitzgerald said with a smile. Stop by the Piedmont Police Department lobby to read or donate a book.

articles.text: Substitute teachers in Piedmont School District received an early Christmas present. At the September 22 school board meeting, they were given a raise from $140 daily to $200, a 43-percent bump in their base pay. The raise aims to make Piedmont more competitive in attracting substitutes, which have been harder to come by in the last two years. The per diem for substitute teachers in 18 public school districts in Alameda County ranges from $130 to $300. Only Dublin was below Piedmont at $130 per day. In comparison, Albany, with roughly 3600 students, compared with Piedmont’s 2600, pays substitute teachers $300 per day, Berkeley pays $225, and Oakland pays $190. The number of new substitute teachers in California has decreased significantly in recent years. The California Commission on Teacher Credentialing issued 64,000 substitute teaching permits statewide for the 2018- 2019 school year. Only 47,000 were issued for the current school year. school year, 13,558 California teachers retired statewide, an increase of 1,000 retirees from the previous year. Fewer teachers and fewer substitutes available has increased the demand for all teachers. In a memorandum to the school board, Booker stated, “Piedmont Unified, like many districts across the state, [is] struggling to secure qualified substitutes. This results in teachers substituting for their colleagues during their prep periods... articles.text: There are a variety of parent language styles that come into play when toddlers are learning how to talk. The way we speak to our children may impact their language learning. Over the years researchers have studied various parent language styles, and some of the conclusions and recommendations are changing. One style which has shown to be beneficial, and has stood the test of time, is repetition of language input to the child. That is, repeated exposure to new words and sentences is key for language learning. Children need to hear new words and sentences repeatedly, and in multiple situations, before they understand, remember and eventually try to use them. One style which was historically thought to be beneficial is telegraphic speech, where the parent uses speech that includes key words that carry most of the meaning in a sentence but removes the grammatical words and endings. For example, “Daddy go out”, “in box”). Early research suggested that parental use of telegraphic speech may benefit children who are learning to talk as it may be easier for children to imitate and learn language when they hear only the key words. But this prevailing wisdom is being challenged. Newer studies are suggesting a different scenario with regard to parent language modeling. When looking at grammatical (grammatical language models include the small grammatical words and word endings) vs. telegraphic parent language styles, recent research concludes that children can imitate short, grammatical sentences as easily as they can imitate telegraphic speech. Furthermore, grammatical sentences are not more difficult for children to understand than telegraphic speech and likely offers an advantage for language learning. Parents who provide short, grammatically correct sentences to their children may be providing valuable clues as to what words mean and how they can be used (for example, “Daddy is going out.”, “in the box”). By including grammatical markers such as “the” the child is learning to pair articles with nouns, and by including grammatical markers such as “-ing” the child is learning to pair word endings with verbs. So how do parents optimally approach talking to children who are learning to talk? First, we say a bit less, keeping our sentences short but grammatical. Next, we use vocal stress (think: a little louder and more animated) to make key words stand out to highlight the salient message. We slow our speech a bit. Speaking slightly (only slightly) slower than you would when speaking to an adult allows the child time to process what you are saying. Make sure to maintain your natural speaking rhythm. Fourth, it is always a good strategy to incorporate visuals when talking to children who are learning to talk. Showing the child that a word means via pointing, using a gesture or an action, or holding up an object or picture enhances language learning. And finally, we provide repetition of our language models over time and across contexts/situations to build children’s conceptualization of language and efficacy of communication. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C . of heart and spirit.

articles.text: Six students from Piedmont High School recently were named National Merit Scholarship semifinalists for 2022, joining a group of students throughout the U.S. with the highest PSAT scores. The students are Aaron Drumm, Charlotte Levy, Anabel Loucks, Chiara Lundin, Charlie Olcott and Robert Sylvia. They are among 16,000 semifinalists and were chosen from a pool of over 1,500,000 high school seniors taking the PSAT. The students will be considered for 7,500 National Merit Scholarships worth a combined $30 million. “It’s very cool to be named a semifinalist along with people that I know and have grown up with. Through PHS courses I have learned how intriguing the functions of the body at the microscopic level are. I hope someday to do research in a field such as genetics or microbiology,” said Lundin. To become a finalist, the student and high school must submit a detailed scholarship application information, academic record, extracurricular activities and awards. They also must submit an essay and earn scores on the SAT comparable to the PSAT. National Merit Scholarship winners will be announced in April 2022.

One style which has shown to be beneficial, and has stood the test of time, is repetition of language input to the child. That is, repeated exposure to new words and sentences is key for language learning. Children need to hear new words and sentences repeatedly, and in multiple situations, before they understand, remember and eventually try to use them. One style which was historically thought to be beneficial is telegraphic speech, where the parent uses speech that includes key words that carry most of the meaning in a sentence but removes the grammatical words and endings. For example, “Daddy go out”, “in box”). Early research suggested that parental use of telegraphic speech may benefit children who are learning to talk as it may be easier for children to imitate and learn language when they hear only the key words. But this prevailing wisdom is being challenged. Newer studies are suggesting a different scenario with regard to parent language modeling. When looking at grammatical (grammatical language models include the small grammatical words and word endings) vs. telegraphic parent language styles, recent research concludes that children can imitate short, grammatical sentences as easily as they can imitate telegraphic speech. Furthermore, grammatical sentences are not more difficult for children to understand than telegraphic speech and likely offers an advantage for language learning. Parents who provide short, grammatically correct sentences to their children may be providing valuable clues as to what words mean and how they can be used (for example, “Daddy is going out.”, “in the box”). By including grammatical markers such as “the” the child is learning to pair articles with nouns, and by including grammatical markers such as “-ing” the child is learning to pair word endings with verbs. So how do parents optimally approach talking to children who are learning to talk? First, we say a bit less, keeping our sentences short but grammatical. Next, we use vocal stress (think: a little louder and more animated) to make key words stand out to highlight the salient message. We slow our speech a bit. Speaking slightly (only slightly) slower than you would when speaking to an adult allows the child time to process what you are saying. Make sure to maintain your natural speaking rhythm. Fourth, it is always a good strategy to incorporate visuals when talking to children who are learning to talk. Showing the child that a word means via pointing, using a gesture or an action, or holding up an object or picture enhances language learning. And finally, we provide repetition of our language models over time and across contexts/situations to build children’s conceptualization of language and efficacy of communication. articles.text: In spite of dry weather and parched vegetation, a full reservoir at Del Valle Regional greeted 37 Scouts and Scout leaders from Piedmont Troop 15 the weekend of September 18-19. Located 10 miles south of Livermore, the park provided excellent swimming and kayaking with the daytime temperature in the low 70’s. Julian Procos said kayaking was his favorite activity, while Davey Ackerman chose fishing and working on advancement requirements. After putting on their backpacks and hiking to the campsite, they set up tents. “It was an amazing camping trip where I learned to set up a tent,” raved Connor Fredericks. “My favorite part was hanging out with my troop. I loved getting to know all of their awesome and unique personalities,” said Christiane Zuber. There was time for play and learning some basic Scout skills. Dinner was prepared from ingredients requiring no refrigeration as a way for Scouts to get used to the type of meals they will prepare on an extended backpacking trip next summer. “My favorite part was cooking food at the end of the day”, said Thalay Visessonchoke. “This was my first time making a meal outdoors with boys and girls about my age”, stated Joaquin Fierro, who has been in Scouting for one month. “I learned how to make a campf ire”, exclaimed Gianluca Richmond. “Making a fire in the evening was my favorite part,” echoed Thomas Ero. During a campfire with songs and toasted marshmallows, a waning gibbous moon emerged from feathery clouds. In the night, a lone coyote barked loudly but briefly. Three turkey vultures glided overhead at dawn to a hillside for leftovers. Del Valle Reservoir provides a refreshingly cool place to swim. Traffic is blocked off at Place Charles de Gaulle, allowing Parisians to stroll the magnificent Boulevard Champs-Elysée during two weekends. The revered Arc de Triomphe is impossible not to gawk at, and now draped in shimmering silvery blue and belted by red rope, it’s an awesome sight. Everyone is puzzling about the near-impossible feat of draping the monument, and, moreover, the question of why. Smart phone-holders are hoisting themselves, precariously, onto street-barriers for a view above people’s heads and “selfies.” Under the changing light of etched puffy clouds moving against a brilliant blue sky, the crowd draws closer to the disorienting view of the monument they’ve known their entire lives. The Arc, the photogenic icon every tourist snaps a picture of, is dolled up in Christo’s favorite Rope workers hanging the silvery blue fabric. go-to fabric, a lightweight polypropylene moving sensuously in the breeze, and reflecting between light and dark under the clouds playfully changing the fabric’s color and folds. This installation, completed posthumously, is his last wrap. The artist known as Christo passed away last year at age 84, prior to the Arc installation. Born in communist Bulgaria in 1935 he left to become an artist in the 50s and 60s, and met his wife and fellow artist Jeanne-Claude. Together they joined the hippest artists abandoning easel painting, pushing boundaries from paint and canvas to radically different forms and materials; elevating light and movement, and techno-crafting, to burst through art’s third dimension. Christo, whose full name was Christo Vladimirov Javacheff, fit into the new Contemporary movement with his novel devotion to being a wrappist or wrapman. He celebrated community and freedom, where he imagined gigantism seemingly impossible to build, but achieved it, however fleeting and temporary. Christo L’Arc de Triomphe, a gift from Christo to Paris. who frequently cited Paris as his favorite city, next to New York, was well accepted before L’Arc de Triomphe, Wrapped. His Pont Neuf Bridge and 44 Street Lamps proved wildly successful in 1985, but he’d spent a decade trying to persuade Paris officials about Pont Neuf, literally the “new” bridge built in 1607, and in daily use by cars and pedestrians. President François Mitterrand cut through the French bureaucracy, and several hundred French laborers signed on, including frogmen, alpinists, and craftsmen of ancient guilds. Fabric has fascinated artists through the ages, and in sculpture, paintings, frescoes or reliefs, artists fashioned fabrics’ folds and pleats using wood, marble, bronze, or plaster. Christo experimented with lacquer to get the desired pleated folds, and with Pont Neuf, he and JeanneClaude draped it with polypropylene fabric, finding the ideal traits for meticulous dressmaker finery that became his standard. The couple’s vision for wrapping Berlin’s Parliament began in 1971, when they and fellow artisans battled for permission through the 70s, 80s, and 90s. Finally, in 1995, they wrapped the Reichstag, the couple’s most important joint project. She died in 2009. French President Emmanuel Macron attended the dedication of L’Arc de Triomphe, Wrapped and remarked, “I think what we believe in is that the wildest of dreams must be possible.” The wrapping of a monument of such historical, military, and national symbolism as an “artistic adventure makes the French people extraordinarily proud.” Wrapping is a complex endeavor, both technical and logistical, where the premise is to do the impossible with precision and the highest degree of perfection, and to amaze the public. The chosen monument (or locality) is contained, its feat celebrated, and then it’s released from the wrappings so painstakingly that it appears untouched. Understandably, this performance art is not meaningful to everyone. A few critics are dismissive as a modern-day folly. Materials used in vast quantities are wasteful environmentally; but Christo recycles most of the materials and declines to fundraise or take public money: the costs are parlayed from his own private fortune; and the Arc is believed to cost €14 million. Inspiration sparked 60 years ago when Christo dwelled in a small room on Avenue Foch with a faraway view to the Arc de Triomphe. The stately arch commissioned by Napoléon in 1806 as a tribute to his military conquests and the French la gloire blended with the agony of war inspired Christo to sketch the wrapping. Piedmont‘s boys’ water polo team thrashed Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco, 17-7, on Thursday, September 23, to improve their record to 11-3 entering the final month of the season. articles.text: A group exhibition showcasing a selection of artworks by eight female artists from the East Bay will open at Piedmont Center for the Arts on October 2. The exhibit, titled 8WA, will be on view Saturdays and Sundays through October 24 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., or by appointment. An artists’ reception will take place Sunday, October 3, from noon to 2 p.m. The exhibition features the work of Laura Abrams, Deborah Green, Michelle Lewis, Laura McNall, Juliet Mevi, Jacqui Rubenstein, Ariella Seidenberg, and Caskey Weston. Over 50 works will be on display. “We appreciate this opportunity to present a self-curated show from our personal collections,“ said Deborah Green, the artist who initiated the project. “I am proud to be part of this group of so many talented and accomplished women, and we are looking forward to exhibiting a strong body of artwork in this beautiful space. It’s especially meaningful to be emerging with a collective show after months of pandemic isolation. Works on display showcase a wide variety of styles and media. Growing out of an association through the Northern California Women’s Caucus for Art, many of the artists here embrace its activist mission with works that put forward dynamic feminist, environmental, and social justice messages.” Gallery hours are free and open to the public, and no reservation is required. articles.text: Filoli House and Garden in Woodside. Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside is celebrating “Orchard Days” every weekend through October 31. Visit the gardens this fall and stroll through the seven-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, a vital component of self-sustaining estates and a feature of many American country houses at the turn of the century. The acres hold a collection of fruits grown for leisure rather than commercial production. The Bourns, the original owners of the estate, planted their orchard with 1,000 trees - to include apples, pears, plums, apricots, walnuts, figs, and quinces. Only 115 trees remained when the orchard was restored, but there are now over 500 fruit and nut trees of various species. Filoli staff preserve the historic collection of rare and historically significant varieties. Fruit picking is not permitted. Access to “Orchard Days” is included with weekend admission tickets. The gardens are open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/orchard-days.

articles.text: Arturo Chacón-Cruz The newest release from San Francisco Opera’s video portrait series, “In Song,” features opera singer Arturo Chacon-Cruz and is now available on YouTube, Facebook, and the opera’s website. From his home in Miami, tenor Chacon-Cruz visits with students at Homestead Mariachi Conservatory in Miami to reveal how culture, determination, and passion shape the music they make together. He performs Agustin Lara’s “Granada” with the students. He also sings Vincenzo De Crescenzo’s “Rondine al Nido” and María Grever’s “Júrame.” Chacon-Cruz is a native of Sonora, Mexico and has established himself in recent years as a leading operatic tenor. He Photo by Karli Evans has performed leading roles at Los Angeles Opera, Washington National Opera, and Carnegie Hall. Earlier this month, he released his newest recording, “De Mi Casa a Tu Casa,” featuring traditional mariachi music. San Francisco Opera’s “In Song” series features intimate video portraits of artists from around the world showcasing a wide variety of genres - from classic to bluegrass, spirituals, Samoan and mariachi. “In Song: J’Nai Bridges,” “In Song: Pene Pati,” and “In Song: Jamie Barton” featuring Béla Fleck, are available on demand on Youtube and the San Francisco Opera website. Upcoming episodes include soprano Amina Edris filmed on location in Egypt. Visit sfopera.com/insong to watch the series.

articles.text: Blues slide guitarist and 2008 Piedmont graduate Jules Leyhe released a new eclectic album, “Your First Rodeo”, on September 17. The album hits a wide range of genres, including blues, funk, big band jazz, and rock, with elements of hip hop and electronica, but each song has his slide guitar leading the way. The Post caught up with Jules for an interview last week. Q: Tell me about the ensemble of musicians on the CD and the instruments we are listening to. A: I mainly play slide guitar on my Gibson SG. We are a traditional blues or funk band, with keyboards, drums, base and a fabulous horn section. Shane Cox, is really the co-captain that is leading the way on trumpet, sousaphone, saxophone and trombone; he does all the horn parts. Q: What went into the decision to make this album totally instrumental without vocals? A: It is like a sonic journey. As much as I love singers, we wanted to tell all the stories with our instruments. I like the less literal meanings of the songs without lyrics; you can derive any kind of meaning you want from these instrumental tunes. We really want to bring attention to the musicians in the band and the creativity of how they are assembled. It is not pop music – it is kind of a wild adventure and an experiment. Q: What is your favorite song on the CD? Piedmont guitarist Jules Leyhe, a graduate of Berklee College of Music, has released his third album, “Your First Rodeo.” Blues slide guitarist and 2008 Piedmont graduate Jules Leyhe A: “The Planetarium” is definitely near and dear to me. There are all these tips of the hat to heroes of mine. The composer Holst produced pieces about all the planets, and our horn themes are a tribute to those. The horns are kind of the call, and the response is the Thin Lizzie or Allman Brothers guitar midis coming back to you. Then it concludes with something like a Jimi Hendrix solo over the rhythm guitar part inspired by “You Never Give Me Your Money,” by the Beatles which is full-on psychedelia. We tried to do it in our style the whole time and not be accused of just copying these great musicians. In four minutes we are throwing all of these things at you in an outer space psychedelic jam. is none of the musicians ever recorded together at the same time. It doesn’t sound like that, though. It sounds pretty natural, like everything goes together. It is amazing that there was never a live take where we all looked at each other, smiled and said, “That’s the one, guys.” And as much as I love Planetarium, it was certainly a challenge to make that not a chaotic storm but a pleasant listening experience. It was definitely tricky to put together. Knowing when to finally say, “Okay it is done,” was like hitting a moving target. Q: What challenges did you face making this CD? I imagined Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s Romance in Fm, Op. 5 as a bossa nova (a soft, romantic Brazilian jazz style). The accompaniment was a typical nylon-string guitar part alternating thumb bass and three-note plucked chords. The melody and improv was electric jazz guitar. The tempo I imagined was “double-time” from the original 70 beats per minute to 135. The melodic rhythm “pushed” most of the notes in the typical floating bossa nova style, playing them before the beat and sustaining them onto the beat. It sounded like Jobim channeling Tchaikovsky. Tchaikovsky’s father was one of the foremost metallurgists in Russia, wealthy enough to provide his seven children a comfortable living and a good education. Tchaikovsky’s mother played piano only well enough to provide music for her children to dance to. No one in his family was a professional musician. Like Art Tatum with his player piano, Tchaikovsky copied musical pieces by ear from the orchestrion on a player piano his Russian composer Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky created the foundation for a range of musical adaptation. father bought him. According to Tchaikovsky’s brother Modeste, he replicated everything he heard on the orchestrion. Tchaikovsky graduated from the Saint Petersburg Conservatory in 1865. Nikolai Rubinstein, a renowned pianist and composer, appointed him as Professor of Music Theory at the Moscow Conservatory in 1866. Tchaikovsky’s text, Guide to the Practical Study of Harmony (1872), provides a good basis for understanding music theory, chord progression and voice leading. In 1868, Tchaikovsky wrote Romance in Fm, Op. 5 and dedicated it to Belgian soprano Désirée Artôt. They were engaged to be married, but Artôt broke it off and married baritone Francisco de Asís Mariano del Carmen Marco Padilla y Ramos, surely for his name! articles.text: First the good news. Holy Names University used to have a respected music school. Sadly, they suffered a severe decline, partly due to the pandemic. The good news is that they have begun to rebuild, beginning with the orchestra. First, they will select a conductor. There are four fine prospects being considered. I attended the first rehearsal and I am happy to report that all is progressing well. On Saturday evening the Quantum Quintet performed a chamber music concert presented by Sunset Music and Arts. The main piece on the program was Dvorak‘s glorious piano quintet. As soon as they began to play, I was transported back in time. It was March 1974 in a small concert hall at USC. The concert was announced as a student recital from the master class of the immortal violinist Jascha Heifetz. The thing to remember here is that it was announced as a student recital. I had an idea that Jascha Heifetz would be one of the performers. The students played one after another in the first half of the program. After intermission, the stage door opened, and out walked Jascha Heifetz and the great cellist Gregory Piatigorsky. Both of these great artists played in the most circumspect manner. They did not want to overshadow their students. This concert was the last they ever played together. What a beautiful memory it was. Time for a recipe from the Gourmet It has been a long time since I offered my readers a recipe. So here goes. CALABRIAN SPAGHETTI Ingredients: spaghetti, a jar of roasted red peppers, smoked salmon, olive oil, anchovy fillets and crushed red pepper flakes. Cook the spaghetti. Combine about 2 ounces per person of the roasted red peppers, and about 2 ounces per person of smoked salmon. Add a little bit of olive oil to moisten and one anchovy per person (use anchovy instead of salt). Add the spaghetti to the other ingredients and heat them together. Stir gently. You can finish the spaghetti with some crushed red pepper flakes for a true Calabrian touch. Do not top with grated Parmesan cheese. Ambrose Bierce And now for something different: Ambrose Bierce was one of the most original writers in American history. His magnum opus, The Devil’s Dictionary, reveals his pugnacious sarcasm to best effect. While there is no information about Bierce’s interest in music, I obtained a document purportedly by Bierce. This “lexicon of musical terms“ has all the earmarks of Bierce’s sharply-pointed humor. Here are a few examples: Piccolo: noun, A small instrument which causes considerable bodily injury. The bane of audiologists. Trombone: noun, the comedian of the orchestra. Given to scatological humor and flatulence. Usually played by mischievous boys who want to annoy girls. Percussion instruments: plural, tone-deaf musicians released on early parole. Some of them become conductors. Violin: noun, when played well, you think you are in heaven. When played badly you think you are in hell. Violin bow: a club made of wood resembling a slender baseball bat and strung with horse hair from the rear end of a horse. Generally used to beat a Violin black and blue. Practice: noun or a verb, an unpleasant hour devoted to repeating your mistakes ad nauseam. Concert: noun, practicing in public. See above. And saving the best for last: Conductor: noun of questionable progeny. Literally the prince of fools. Usually an egotist from highest Valhalla who thinks he knows everything. Despised by members of the orchestra even though they aspire to the position.

articles.text: The 64th Monterey Jazz Festival presented Herbie Hancock, Pat Metheny, Lidesi, George Benson and others in an outdoor event Friday through Sunday last weekend, September 24-26, demonstrating the skill of the masters and the talent of rising stars. DAY ONE Pat Metheny, guitarist extraordinaire, and Side Eye, his new project, opened the Festival. Metheny’s fluid command rang from guitars that ranged from a vintage jazz box to his 42-string Pikasso as he reworked pieces like “Timeline “ and presented new compositions. He was backed by James Francies on piano whose style blends lighting runs with a strong left hand movement that grounded Metheny’s lyricism. Herbie Hancock, the legendary pianist, played a set that spanned his body of work from grand piano through the “keytar”. He is at his best at the piano, deftly moving through voice led chords with lyric right-hand flights. Elena Pinderhughes, a Berkeley raised flutist and vocalist, was the surprise of the set. Her flute work was virtuosic and her voice shared joy and strength in her compositions such as “Breath in Breath Out”. The melodic tone of her flute was a perfect complement to Hancock’s piano. DAY TWO Japanese born composer Miho Hazama and her orchestra opened the day with a program of lush orchestral jazz suites including the three-movement “It’s A Planet” commissioned by the Festival. Hazama’s style is lyric and often involves reeds-based jazz riffs emerging from a sweeping wave of strings. Legendary drummer Terri Herbie Hancock Lynn Carrington and Social Science presented a program of rhythm-driven jazz tuned to a theme of social justice in songs such as “Bells”. The jewel of the combo was vocalist Debo Reyes whose soaring and soulful style brought a lyric and haunting tone to the set. Ledisi closed the evening in an electrifying vocal performance. Fresh from her 2021 Grammy Award, Ledisi (LEDes-see) showed herself to be a musical Diva in the best sense of the word: commanding, vulnerable and effortlessly virtuosic. She worked through songs from her CDs including “Anything for You”. However, the most moving piece was her balladic mixture of Nina Simone’s “Baltimore” with her own composition “Shot Down” that created a haunting anthem of social justice. She was the apex of the Festival. DAY THREE Pianist Christian Sands, the Festival’s artist in residence, opened on Sunday with a quartet that focused on his new CD “Be Water”. Sands’ seamless voice leading and fluid lyric style led the audience through the spiritual journey that was the source of this project. Kandace Springs (vocal/ piano) then returned us to the American songbook as she played a set that moved from “Angel Eyes” to “I Put a Spell On You”. A gifted stylist, she made each song her own as her voice and piano often seemed to act as one instrument. George Benson closed the festival as people rose, cheered and danced. As Benson played his many hits, the audience was reminded of the quality of his vocal style that ranges from soft crooning to happy scatting. His bright staccato guitar style is still evident; however closing the Festival before a familiar audience one felt they were listening to Nat Cole or Johnny Hartman – a mature stylistic voice that will live in the history of jazz. The Monterey Festival, like the Piedmont Jazz Festival one week earlier, was not only a celebration of jazz, but the indomitable spirit of musical creation after a long uncertainty. George Benson

DAY TWO Japanese born composer Miho Hazama and her orchestra opened the day with a program of lush orchestral jazz suites including the three-movement “It’s A Planet” commissioned by the Festival. Hazama’s style is lyric and often involves reeds-based jazz riffs emerging from a sweeping wave of strings. Legendary drummer Terri Herbie Hancock Lynn Carrington and Social Science presented a program of rhythm-driven jazz tuned to a theme of social justice in songs such as “Bells”. The jewel of the combo was vocalist Debo Reyes whose soaring and soulful style brought a lyric and haunting tone to the set. Ledisi closed the evening in an electrifying vocal performance. Fresh from her 2021 Grammy Award, Ledisi (LEDes-see) showed herself to be a musical Diva in the best sense of the word: commanding, vulnerable and effortlessly virtuosic. She worked through songs from her CDs including “Anything for You”. However, the most moving piece was her balladic mixture of Nina Simone’s “Baltimore” with her own composition “Shot Down” that created a haunting anthem of social justice. She was the apex of the Festival. DAY THREE Pianist Christian Sands, the Festival’s artist in residence, opened on Sunday with a quartet that focused on his new CD “Be Water”. Sands’ seamless voice leading and fluid lyric style led the audience through the spiritual journey that was the source of this project. Kandace Springs (vocal/ piano) then returned us to the American songbook as she played a set that moved from “Angel Eyes” to “I Put a Spell On You”. A gifted stylist, she made each song her own as her voice and piano often seemed to act as one instrument. George Benson closed the festival as people rose, cheered and danced. As Benson played his many hits, the audience was reminded of the quality of his vocal style that ranges from soft crooning to happy scatting. His bright staccato guitar style is still evident; however closing the Festival before a familiar audience one felt they were listening to Nat Cole or Johnny Hartman – a mature stylistic voice that will live in the history of jazz. The Monterey Festival, like the Piedmont Jazz Festival one week earlier, was not only a celebration of jazz, but the indomitable spirit of musical creation after a long uncertainty. 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org READ IT IN THE POST George Benson

articles.text: Thomasin McKenzie and Alex Wolff in Old. First things first: I have yet to watch Old, written and directed by M. Night Shyamalan (Sixth Sense, Signs, Split), and now debuting in walk-in theaters; but then I haven’t been inside a local movie house for well over a year. When I heard about the premise of Old, adapted from Sandcastle, a French graphic novel, I immediately Googled it and screened the trailer more than a few times. Not infrequently, a trailer will reveal more than is necessary. This one doesn’t. It just manages to intrigue, even captivate, offering just enough of the plot to create that familiar Shyamalan sense of dread, an emotion that threads through all of his films, with greater effect in some than others. In Old we are introduced to tropical vacationers (a family of four, plus others), who are encouraged by their hotel concierge to visit a remote, secluded beach: white sand, blue water, it seems idyllic. At first the kids discover strange artifacts in the sand (cracked sunglasses). The body of a woman floats toward a swimmer. And then they begin to age. Suddenly the film becomes a meditation on the passage of time. Something is happening. What that thing is, is desperately inexplicable, an impenetrable mystery. And so, the audience is asked to walk through a creepy portal without any exposition that explains what is happening. Or so I assume. Embedded in the plot is the awareness by Shyamalan that our culture (western, European) is obsessed with longevity (diet, prophylactic drugs, exercise), anything that will slow, resist, push back the aging process. We are all dimly aware that there was a time when life expectancy was a mere fraction of what it is today. In the middle 18th century, one’s life span was some 35 years. By 1918 it was 54. Today it is 80, thanks to the miracle of a host of vaccines (smallpox shots, for example), and a bunch of metaphorical, modern medicine seat belts. So to watch Old is to contemplate how time can seem strangely distorted (the pandemic has twisted time in some weird ways), and begs the question whether what Shyamalan has created is a fable for this peculiar moment. Old. Written and directed by M. Night Shyamalan. Starring Gael Garcia Bernal, Alex Wolff, Victoria Kriepa. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: News of the World is an extraordinary, elegiac neo-western adapted from the Paulette Jules 2016 novel. It is set in Texas in 1870, three years after the end of the Civil War. Confederate veteran Captain Jefferson Kyle Kidd (Tom Hanks), once a printer, now makes his improbable living by travelling from to town om Texas reading the news – stories gleaned from newspapers from both near and far, standing stage center in candle-lit rooms, saying, “I read the news to anyone with ten cents and the time to hear it.” His audience is comprised of rough-hewn settlers, many still coming to terms with the defeat of the South. Many of those standing before him either can’t read, or spend every waking hour in physical labor; yet, all remain eager to hear the news of the world. As we soon come to realize, Captain Kidd is not only a respected man of letters, but also a storyteller and entertainer, and an enthusiastic, at times jocular reader of what could simply be the dry words on a page of newsprint. His mission is not only to inform but to capture the imaginations of his audience. On a trip to another town he discovers an overturned wagon on the side of the road. Investigating, he sees the body of a black freedman, hanging from a tree. Hiding nearby, among the brush, he spots a terrified young white girl (Helena Zengel), 12, dressed in Native American clothes, her blond hair bluntly cut. She is able to speak only Kiowa. He discovers some identifying papers in the wagon that say that she is German, her name is Johanna (she later explains that she is called Cicada), and she was abducted as a youngster and her parents were killed. A passing Union patrol captain, after examining the documents, instructs Kidd to take her to the next town where the Bureau of Indian Affairs will arrange to return her to her surviving family, now living in a settlement called Castroville. Reluctantly, he agrees. And so begins an episodic journey where he and Johanna develop a halting bond, despite their inability to fully communicate. Theirs is a road trip through an unstable Texas, across dry plains, stopping in raw, muddy towns filled with gritty, bitter men who resent the presence of Union soldiers, constant reminders of the fact that they lost the war. When Captain Kidd learns that the head of Indian Affairs will not be back for some three months, he is at a loss as what to do with Johanna. But he finally realizes that if she is ever to be reunited with her relatives, it is up to him to help find them. News of the World is a remarkable narrative featuring two people who struggle to move beyond trauma. It is also a wonderful, deeply human character study that is aesthetically striking, stunningly authentic, and photographed beautifully by cinematographer Darius Wolski. The performances by Hanks and Zengel are impressively nuanced and touchingly moving. While spare, the story also makes subtle connections to today’s moment in history in which acrimonious divisions continue to haunt us. News of the World. Now streaming. Directed by Paul Greengrass. Starring Tom Hanks, Helena Zengel, Elizabeth Marvel. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Antz feature the voice acting of Woody Allen and Sharon Stone. Antz was the first animated feature created by Dreamworks studio. By design it is a hybrid of sorts, intended to appeal to children age 8 and up, as well as older audiences. The story opens with Ant Z4195 (Woody Allen), a sixlegged neurotic, stretched out on his shrink’s couch, kvetching about the injustice of his life on the anthill. To begin with, he hates dirt, is dissatisfied with being a member of a huge colony, was abandoned by his father when he was just a larva, can’t lift 10 times his weight, and is the middle child in a family of five million. You can hear Woody bringing his signature shtick from the streets of Manhattan to Antz. So here we go: Z is at an ant bar when princess Bala (Sharon Stone), aristocratic daughter of the Queen (Ann Bancroft), decides to go slumming and spend an evening with the worker ants. Z is smitten with the princess, asks her to dance, and the two shock the bar denizens with their own outrageous, freewheeling version of a line dance to the song Guantanamera. Z can’t get Bala out of his mind, and hearing that there will be a military parade passing in front of the royal stands, and hoping to get a glimpse of the princess, he convinces his good friend soldier ant Weaver (Sylvester Stallone) to loan him his helmet so he can join the parade and march with the other soldiers. Meanwhile, the deranged General Mandible (Gene Hackman) is devising a plan to preemptively attack the termites (five times the size of the ants). He manages to convince the queen to support his declaration of war. His hidden objective is to take over the entire anthill. To his consternation, Z is swept into battle with the other soldier ants. The question is, will Z survive, and ultimately win the heart of the fair maiden Bala, who has shared with Z that she also is not happy with her life either. They have even dreamed of escaping to Insectopia (a nearby New York trashcan) where they can live happily ever after. Well, almost. There is a funny scene where the two are stuck to a wad of bubblegum, which is stuck to the bottom of an enormous tennis shoe. Antz is an amusing, witty adventure with some wicked dialogue that touches on the tension that exists between being a conformist or free thinker, all while encouraging the audience to root for the underdog. Actually, it’s hard not to care about these speck-sized creatures, especially Woody as Z. Antz. Animation-adventure. Directed by Eric Darnell. With the voices of Woody Allen, Sharon Stone, and Gene Hackman. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: To begin with, kids are going to enjoy a Bug’s Life. It’s a superb, animated feature filled with a creepy-crawly menagerie of bugs, inspired by a well-known Aesop’s Fable, The Ant and the Grasshopper. The story opens with a wonderfully natural-looking colony of ants that makes its home on a mound of dirt, near a creek bed. It’s known as Ant Island and is ruled by the Queen ant and her daughter, Princess Atta (Julia Louis-Dreyfus). As we soon learn, every summer a gang of thuggish grasshoppers arrive, led by the swaggering Hopper (Kevin Spacey). They demand to be given food collected by the hard-working colony. A nerdy ant named Flik (Dave Foley), a young tinkerer, has an accident while trying to invent a conveyor belt to move seeds intended for the grasshoppers. When the gadget malfunctions, he knocks the gathered food into the water. Whoops. Hopper is furious, and he demands that the ants give him twice as much food as promised, to make up for the loss. Flik, rebelling and feeling bullied, insists that the demand for double the rations is wrong, and suggests to the Queen that he leave and find warrior type bugs, to help the colony in a fight against the grasshoppers. Enough is enough. Princess Atta, apparently not a fan of Flik, encourages him, assuming it’s unlikely that he will return alive from his mission. Flik journeys to Bug City (a heap of trash piled under a trailer), and it is there that he recruits a cohort of “warriors”. In reality they are actually a troupe of Circus Bugs recently fired by ringmaster P.T. Flea (John Ratzenberger). Having no idea what they are getting into, they agree to return to Ant Hill with Flik, who they assume is a talent scout. When they arrive at the colony, they discover what is afoot, and they are not there to perform. Flik pleads with them to stay and pretend to be what they’re not: fighters, not entertainers. Meanwhile, having discovered that the grasshoppers are afraid of birds, Flik sets about building a giant bird, hoping it will be a kind of scarecrow, and scare off Hopper and his gang. And so this engaging story continues, with one confrontation after another, all while introducing an imaginative coterie of bugs. There’s pill bug, a black widow spider, a praying mantis, a walking stick, a large caterpillar, and a male ladybug. Even P.T. Flea makes an appearance, just to keep things interesting. Flik convinces his assembled crew, which includes his fellow ants, that they outnumber the grasshoppers and have the ability to drive the invaders away – which they do, with the exception of Hopper. And so, Flik, the geeky ant and gadgeteer, saves the Hill and the day, and can now invent whatever he wants. A Bug’s Life. Pixar animation. Directed by John Lasseter. With voices of Dave Foley, Kevin Spacey, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated G. EPISCOPAL CHURCH

articles.text: Part 29 of a biweekly series In my experience, the most difficult part of painting buildings is not finding the painting contractor, not the scraping, sanding or surface preparation, not dealing with the mess. The most difficult part is the selection of colors. Maybe this is because like most aspects of the architectural field, color selection is a curious mix of art and science, and…we all experience colors differently. Balancing the main color attributes of hue (color: red, blue, etc.), intensity (saturation or purity), and value (lightness/ Photos by Will Adams A variation on the classical color wheel fashioned by Sir Isaac Newton in 1666 that we all learned in grammar school. Although modern physics reveals variants on the principles involved, they still hold true when mixing paint. Colorists continue to use the color wheel to determine harmonious color combinations. darkness i.e., tints/shades) with other associated variables is simply a difficult job. In the end, from the bold, emotion-evoking colors of Mexican architects such as the famous Luis Barragan, to the restrained, subtle colors we are most familiar with in the Bay Area, exterior colors on a building reveal, perhaps more than anything else, the attitudes, ideas and personality of the owners. Building colors should first respond to the character, style, and detailing of the architecture. Schemes with multiple colors require a natural stopping/starting point for color changes such as a different material or corners and offsets in wall planes. Certain interior colors need also be coordinated, most notably curtains and shades which are seen through the windows and have to work with the exterior colors. Because all urban buildings are surrounded by neighboring buildings, as well as landscape planting, paving, and other elements, exterior color selection necessarily also involves urban design considerations; each building is part of a larger neighborhood palate. Evaluation of color requires certain steps to be successful. Most importantly, although not nearly done often enough, is to allow enough time for color selection and approval before painting starts. Once an attitude and concept is settled upon, selection begins with little paint chips – only the first step. Many architectural offices specify that large (100 sf) samples then be painted on at least two different walls of the building with different natural light conditions. These must be allowed to dry for at least a few days before being evaluated. It is good for owners to then reflect on the samples at different times of the day for a good week before modifications are made or final approval given. This is all pretty complex, at least to me. If it’s one thing I’ve learned is that professional help (and patience) is essential in color selection. Color is mysterious, and what it does to the psyche is diverse. But the measure of success is simple in the end. It is the answer to the question: do you like it? Does it make you glad to be at that place? Does it, as Marie Kondo would ask, bring you joy? articles.text: The Oakland Zoo returned to one of its most popular traditions last Saturday, September 25, allowing visitors to help feed the animals. Last year’s Feast for the Beasts was cancelled, so the zoo created an event called Brunch For The Wild Bunch this year, with giraffes, baboons, elephants, and grizzly bears the lucky winners of a free meal. The animal feeding consisted of four areas where guests were able to go into the enclosures and spread out food for the animals. The event was sold out, so I went as an onlooker and writer. I walked around the zoo watching what the animals who didn’t get a feeding were eating at that time. To my surprise, the most discarded food was lettuce. Curious about why lettuce leaves were being tossed back on the ground or left uneaten, I turned to Isabella Linares, a Marketing Associate for the answer. She explained that some animals are quite picky. With lemurs, as example, the females eat first in their hierarchy. They will eat all the fruits first and leave the rest for the males. But whatever they don’t eat they will save for later. On Saturday all the animals were eating at a specific time of the day, but on a normal day or week it will depend on the animal. Grizzly bears will eat 16 times a day when getting ready to hibernate, a process known as hyperphagia. Saturday’s meals A Grant’s Zebra was a show-stopper for avid photographers. But whatever they don’t eat they will save for later. On Saturday all the animals were eating at a specific time of the day, but on a normal day or week it will depend on the animal. Grizzly bears will eat 16 times a day when getting ready to hibernate, a process known as hyperphagia. Saturday’s meals Staff photos A pride of three African lions roams a hilly, forested habitat at the Oakland Zoo. When thy roar, all visitors and animals at the zoo, pay attention. A large number of visitors were allowed to spread food in the elephant and giraffe habitat at Oakland Zoo on Saturday for the zoo’s Feast Day for animals. A curious sight was seeing hundreds of people watching other people inside the elephant enclosure placing for the animals to eat – at a later time. were all a smaller size – more like a snack. Birds will eat two times a day and will be satisfied. Getting down to what the animals enjoy eating, it all depends on the type of animal and its habitat. I think that the Oakland Zoo is a perfect example of that, because it is always finding new ways to bring the community together.

This book has a clear autobiographical bent: Alice is a young novelist who has rocketed to worldwide fame. Her close friendship with Eileen anchors the book, with their email exchanges alighting on everything from political and social upheaval to their romantic lives. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. The Wrong End of the Telescope, by Rabih Alameddine Mina, a trans Lebanese American doctor, arrives in Lesbos to volunteer at a refugee camp, and the experience takes on an unexpectedly personal dimension after she meets Sumaiya, a Syrian woman trying to hide the extent of her illness from her family. Grove Press. Chronicles From the Land of the Happiest People on Earth, by Wole Soyinka The Nobel laureate’s first novel in nearly 50 years reads like a sendup of an imaginary Nigeria, equally a mystery and political satire, centered on a black market for human flesh and the doctor trying to get to the bottom of what’s going on. Pantheon Books. won a Pulitzer Prizes for The Underground Railroad and The Nickel Boys, a rich, wild book. Doubleday. Palmares, by Gayl Jones It’s been two decades since Jones released a new novel, and she returns with a multipart series centered on Almeyda, a young enslaved girl in colonial Brazil, who makes her way to a utopia where Black people are free. After the settlement is destroyed, Almeyda crosses the country in search of her lost husband. Beacon Press. Bewilderment, by Richard Powers As with his Pulitzer Prize-winning novel The Overstory, Powers’s new book encourages readers to look beyond ourselves. A widowed father, Theo, is an astrobiologist researching the possibility of life throughout the galaxy. His son, Robin, is struggling with outbursts at school and difficult emotions, but finds relief in an experimental neurofeedback therapy, which allows him to access his dead mother’s feelings. W. W. Norton & Company Inseparable, by Simone de Beauvoir. Translated by Sandra Smith. De Beauvoir may be most closely associated with Jean-Paul Sartre, but this loosely autobiographical novel, written in 1954 and put aside for decades, suggests that her more significant relationship was with her childhood friend Zaza. Ecco. This time, she focuses on the Delaney family, headed by two retired tennis stars, and the fallout after their mother goes missing. Henry Holt & Co. articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I don’t really need a new phone, as I have an iPhone 11. I am a hobbyist photographer, and I do like to take pictures and especially videos with my phone. I am hearing some good things about the new iPhone that just came out. Are you recommending the newest iPhone? My phone works fine, but the battery gives out by late afternoon, especially when I use the camera a lot. So, I am really tempted just to get a new iPhone. Lowell F., Piedmont Dear Lowell: Since you like to take pictures and videos, I would say this is a fine time to get the iPhone 13. If you are shooting a lot of videos on your current phone, this could be the cause of your battery draining. It seems that the camera capabilities on the last couple of phones have increased so much, that I hardly ever use my DSLR for landscape scenes. When I travel for wildlife photo trips, I use my long lens for animals and birds, and my iPhone for beautiful sunsets and scenery. There are many times I have used my phone just to frame a shot, and then realized the results are so spectacular that there is no need to pull out my DSLR. I must say that I see many photographers, both hobbyists and pros, enjoying the photo capabilities of the newer iPhones. As far as the iPhone 13 which just became available on September 24, there are 4 models: the iPhone 13, 13 Mini, 13 Pro, and 13 Pro Max. Personally, I upgraded to the 13 Pro Max from a 12 Pro Max, because the 13 is reported to have better battery life, 2.5 hours longer than its predecessor. And I can attest that this is true, as by the end of today, after using the map, email, messages, taking several photos and a few videos, the battery is at 69% this evening. And of course, the new camera features also drew me in. Since you mentioned that you enjoy taking pictures and videos with your phone, there are some features with this new model that I think you will like. Here is a list of a few of the ones I am excited about: 1. Cinematic Mode: This is a video mode which automatically switches the focus between subjects to give footage a more filmlike aesthetic. You can tap on a subject to switch focus and tap twice to hold focus on that subject. 2. Wide Angle and Night Mode: Like the previous iPhone Apples’ new iPhone 13 and 13 mini. 12 Pro Max, the iPhone 13 uses sensor shift technology for stabilization and also has a much wider aperture and improved (over the iPhone 12) night mode for better shots in the dark. 3. Macro Function: The super wide lens also has a new macro function which allows you to shoot objects less than an inch away from the lens. 4. Telephoto Zoom: This has been increased to 3x, up from 2.5x of the 12 Pro. 5. Apple ProRes: This is an Apple developed video codec that allows you to shoot at 4K resolution at 30 frames per second, a feature available on the 13 Pro and Pro Max. As far as the question about when to upgrade to a new device, I always ask, “What kinds of things do you do on your phone?” If you use the camera a lot, these improvements are worth it, in my mind. The main camera on this new phone has a larger image sensor with a f/1.5 aperture which is why it can let in more light to facilitate better lo light and night mode shooting. But if you just use your phone as a phone, there is no need to upgrade if your model is only a couple of models behind the current one. When you are ready to purchase, make sure to check with your carrier, as they often have better deals than Apple. Apple, as well as many of the carriers have an “upgrade every year” program, where the cost of the phone is split into 24 monthly interest free payments. After you have paid for 12 months, you can turn the phone in for the newer model. Even if your model is a few years old, most carriers and Apple will give you some trade in credit towards the cost of a new phone. Since the phones just came out you should be prepared to wait a few weeks for delivery. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com.

articles.text: Several years ago I read about a community for older adults in the Netherlands that allows university students to live there rentfree. What a deal. In exchange for a small apartment, the students do a variety of activities with the older residents, including watching sports together, celebrating birthdays and, perhaps most importantly, offering personal interaction and companionship to seniors. Here in the United States, intergenerational programs have become a growing trend within senior living. As we emerge from the confines of Covid-19, we can attest to the value of both intergenerational programming as well as intergenerational living communities. The pandemic forced multiple generations of families to live together, to rely on each other as jobs were lost, school was canceled. Younger family members were able to assist their older relatives. The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living is on the leading edge of intergenerational programming. Just last week we hosted a reading by the award-winning young writers from the Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Program. It’s an unprecedented citywide effort to celebrate literacy through poetry and connect young writers to far-reaching opportunities. Two of the program’s finalists, Dara Kashayar and Siara Edmond, were participants with us. They read some of their poetry and then were asked questions by our residents and those watching online. Siara Edmond is a finalist in the Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Program. The first question asked was, “How has interacting with older adults impacted you and your writing?” We got a quick response from Dara who said, “My grandmother and parents emigrated from Iran. Persian culture teaches children to revere the wisdom their elders can impart. This is part of my identity; it definitely impacts my writing.” Another young Oakland poet, Siara, writes poems about her grandparents. “I appreciate the hard work they did in order to better the lives of their children and grandchildren,” she said. For the past five years, The Lake Merritt has initiated an intergenerational program called “Conversation Exchange.” We partner with Laney College students who are learning English as a second language. Students come to The Lake Merritt after classes to meet with our residents and build their English language fluency by conversing on a wide range of topics. This program has been wildly successful and a win-win for both students and our Dara Kashayar, a finalist in the Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Program, read his poetry to Lake Merritt Senior Living residents. residents. Our resident Mary met Etta, a Chinese student through the program. Mary said, “I love working with Etta. Our meetings together are valuable to both of us. She is so bright and her English gets better all the time. It’s a good feeling knowing I have had a hand in helping her,” Mary added. In a world seemingly more divided each day, intergenerational programs offer connective solutions that benefit everyone. According to the California Health Report, intergenerational programming is a solution for two problems at once: kids get the attention they crave – sparking better performance at school – while their elder counterparts enjoy improved emotional and physical health. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, at 1800 Madison Street in Oakland. For more information call 510- 903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: In the Christian Scriptures the Apostle Paul refers to believers as “co-creators with God.” The troubles we face should not be signs of failure alone, but also as opportunities for growth. If a structure excludes others from the advantages we have enjoyed, perhaps it’s time to rip out a wall or two and expand our vision to include all. Perhaps it’s another time in our history to see opportunity in the chaos and blessing in the struggle. As we approach Thanksgiving, let us be cautious about what we are thankful for. I suppose it’s only human practice what I call “comparative gratitude”, that is, being thankful for things we have that others do not. But Jesus actually defined blessings as challenges. In his most famous sermon on the mount, he said, “Blessed are the hungry, blessed are those who mourn, and blessed are those who are persecuted...” One could argue that it is a very un-Christian thing to define a blessing as something we have that others do not. Jesus understood blessings as challenges that open us up to more profoundly rely on each other and inspire us to rebuild together. Perhaps we should allow our “comparative gratitude” to disturb us in a way that leads to action, rather than lull us into complacency. So if a blessing is something that draws us toward a new and larger vision, maybe we should be thankful, not only for what we have now, but also for the opportunity to create and build something more inclusive, more peaceful, more beautiful, that might be described as one nation under God. Perhaps this understanding of what a real blessing is will help us not be discouraged by chaos, but rather, inspire us to pick up our shovels, hammers and levels and begin to build a better future for all. Piedmont schools rank among the top public schools in California, but this level of excellence comes at a financial cost. As the costs have increased, government funding has remained nearly flat, resulting in a funding gap of $2,140 per Piedmont student, the difference between what it costs to give students a top-notch education and the amount that Piedmont public schools receive from the state and local parcel taxes. “Piedmont schools would look very different without Giving Campaign contributions.
